title: How to write tests
summary: The anatomy of a test function, assert!, assert_eq! and assert_ne!, custom failure messages, testing for panics with should_panic, and tests that return Result.

sections: TRPL 11.1 Testing Equality with assert_eq! and assert_ne!
TRPL 11.1 Checking for Panics with should_panic
TRPL 11.1 Using Result<T, E> in Tests

blocks.md:
Edsger Dijkstra wrote that testing can show the presence of bugs, but never their absence. The type system catches a whole class of mistakes, but it cannot know that `add_two(2)` should be `4`. **Tests** check that: they run your code with known inputs and compare the result with what you expect.

You have been running tests all course long: every exercise is checked by a test file. Now you learn to write them.

blocks.title: The anatomy of a test
blocks.md:
A test is an ordinary function marked with the **`#[test]`** attribute. `cargo test` builds a special test binary that runs every such function and reports which passed and which failed. A test **fails if it panics**; otherwise it passes.

`cargo new adder --lib` creates a library with a test already in `src/lib.rs`:

blocks.explain: `#[cfg(test)]` compiles the `tests` module only when testing, so it costs nothing in the real build. `use super::*;` brings the parent module's items, here `add`, into scope. Exercises in this course use the same layout, with the tests in their own file `src/tests.rs`.

blocks.explain: Each test is listed with its path (`tests::it_works`) and result. *ignored*, *measured* and *filtered out* are explained in the next lesson. *Doc-tests* are examples in documentation comments, compiled and run as tests (lesson 3).

blocks.md: When a test fails, the output shows which one and why:

blocks.code:
running 2 tests
test tests::exploration ... ok
test tests::another ... FAILED

failures:

---- tests::another stdout ----

thread 'tests::another' panicked at src/lib.rs:17:9:
Make this test fail
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace

failures:
    tests::another

test result: FAILED. 1 passed; 1 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.00s

blocks.title: Assertion macros
rows: as above, but only in debug builds

blocks.explain: These are the checks from *The Rust Programming Language*, run in `main` here so you can see them pass. In a test file each would be its own `#[test]` function. Assertion macros work anywhere, not only in tests.

blocks.title: Left and right
blocks.md: `assert_eq!` does not care which argument is the expected value; failures print them as `left` and `right`. To compare your own types, they need `PartialEq` (for the comparison) and `Debug` (for the message): `#[derive(PartialEq, Debug)]`.

blocks.code:
---- tests::it_adds_two stdout ----

thread 'tests::it_adds_two' panicked at src/lib.rs:12:9:
assertion `left == right` failed
  left: 5
 right: 4
blocks.explain: What a failing `assert_eq!(add_two(2), 4)` prints when `add_two` wrongly adds 3.

blocks.title: Let the assertions find the bug
blocks.md: `median` has a bug, and one of the assertions in `main` catches it. Run it, read the `left`/`right` values in the panic message, and fix `median` (not the assertions).
blocks.task: Fix median so every assertion passes and the program prints `ok`.
hints: The failing assertion says `left: Some(3.0)`, `right: Some(2.5)`. Which case does the code not handle?
For an even length, average `v[mid - 1]` and `v[mid]`.

blocks.title: Testing that code panics
blocks.md: Sometimes the correct behavior **is** a panic, like `Guess::new(200)` from chapter 9. Add **`#[should_panic]`** under `#[test]`: the test passes if the function panics and fails if it does not. Plain `should_panic` passes for any panic, even an unrelated one, so add **`expected = "..."`** with a substring of the message you expect:

blocks.explain: If the two `panic!` messages were swapped by mistake, `Guess::new(200)` would still panic, but with the wrong message, and the test would fail with `panic did not contain expected string`.

blocks.title: Tests that return Result
Make the tests pass
blocks.goal: Read a test file as a specification, including should_panic tests and tests that return Result, and implement code that satisfies it.
blocks.behavior:
Read `src/tests.rs` first: it is the specification. Implement:
- `pub fn clamp_percent(v: i32) -> u8`: clamps to 0..=100.
- `pub struct Temperature { kelvin: f64 }` with `pub fn from_kelvin(k: f64) -> Temperature` that **panics** with a message containing `"below absolute zero"` for `k < 0.0`, and `pub fn celsius(&self) -> f64`.
- `pub fn parse_kv(s: &str) -> Result<(String, i32), String>`: `"key=12"` gives `("key", 12)`; no `=` gives `Err("missing =")`; a bad number gives `Err("bad number")`; an empty key gives `Err("empty key")`. Spaces around key and value are trimmed.
blocks.solution_explain: The test file told you everything: the exact error strings, the panic message fragment, and the trimming. Reading tests as a specification is a skill in itself; it is how you learn an unfamiliar codebase fast.

questions.q: When does a Rust test fail?
options: When it takes longer than 1 second
questions.explanation: No panic and no Err means a pass.

questions.q: What does `#[cfg(test)]` on the tests module do?
options: Runs the tests at compile time
Compiles the module only for `cargo test`
questions.explanation: The code is left out of normal builds.

questions.q: Your struct is compared with `assert_eq!`. What must it implement?
questions.explanation: PartialEq for ==, Debug to print the values on failure.

options: So the test only passes if the panic message contains that text, not for any panic
questions.explanation: A panic for the wrong reason should not count as a pass.

questions.q: A test returning `Result<(), String>` can use `?`.

points: A test is a `#[test]` function; it fails if it panics.
Put unit tests in a `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` with `use super::*;`.
`assert!`, `assert_eq!` and `assert_ne!` check conditions; add a message after the arguments.
`#[should_panic(expected = "...")]` tests that code panics with the right message.
Tests may return `Result<(), E>` and use `?`.

terms.def: The attribute that marks a function as a test for cargo test to run.
A macro that panics, printing both values, if its two arguments are not equal.
A test attribute that makes a test pass only if the code panics (optionally with a given message).
Conditional compilation: the item is compiled only when building tests.
